clinicalPearls: A full-thickness defect through the nasal septum whose causes span iatrogenic, traumatic, inflammatory, and toxic aetiologies
Prior septal surgery is the commonest cause, followed by digital trauma, intranasal cocaine use, and topical vasoconstrictor or steroid overuse
Anterior perforations tend to produce whistling, crusting, epistaxis, and obstruction, whereas posterior perforations may be silent
Cocaine abuse and systemic vasculitis, particularly granulomatosis with polyangiitis, are important causes to exclude, along with malignancy
A saddle-nose deformity or extension beyond the septum suggests a destructive vasculitic, infective, or neoplastic process rather than simple trauma
Small symptomatic perforations may be managed conservatively with saline irrigation, emollients, and a Silastic septal button, while surgical repair is offered for suitable defects
The margins should be examined and biopsied when an underlying inflammatory, infective, or malignant cause is suspected
reference.pathophysiology: A nasal septal perforation develops when the mucoperichondrium is disrupted on both sides of the septum and the intervening cartilage or bone, deprived of its blood and nutrient supply, necroses and is lost. Iatrogenic injury during septal surgery, repetitive digital trauma, and the intense vasoconstriction produced by cocaine or overused topical decongestants all compromise mucosal perfusion. Inflammatory and granulomatous diseases such as vasculitis, and infiltrative malignancy, destroy the septal framework directly. Once a perforation is established, turbulent airflow across its edges causes drying, crusting, and repeated mucosal breakdown, which tends to enlarge the defect and produces the characteristic crusting, bleeding, whistling, and obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other vasculitides
Chronic granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis or syphilis
additionalInvestigations: Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to size and site the perforation and inspect the margins
Biopsy of the perforation edges where an inflammatory, infective, or neoplastic cause is suspected
Vasculitis screen including antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
Investigations for granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis and syphilis serology
CT of the sinuses to assess bony involvement and extent of any destructive process
redFlags: Progressive destruction with a developing saddle-nose deformity, suggesting vasculitis, infection, or malignancy
Systemic features of vasculitis such as pulmonary or renal involvement
An enlarging or ulcerating lesion with atypical margins raising concern for malignancy
A history of cocaine use with ongoing midfacial tissue loss
reference.prognosis: Many small perforations remain stable and are well controlled with conservative measures or a septal button, and carefully selected defects can be repaired successfully, but the outlook worsens when the cause is an ongoing destructive vasculitis, infection, cocaine use, or malignancy.
pitfalls: Assuming a perforation is postsurgical or traumatic without excluding vasculitis, cocaine use, or malignancy
Failing to biopsy suspicious margins and missing an underlying disease
Attempting surgical repair while a destructive process or ongoing cocaine use remains active
Overlooking systemic vasculitic involvement that requires urgent medical management
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
